opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, and I don't think there's one right answer yet. A natural first instinct is to say the model should act like a doctor, because that's the most familiar template we have for medical expertise. But I'm not sure that's quite right, and it might even be limiting.

When you see a physician, you get a lot of good things: deep knowledge, clinical judgment, a sense of accountability. You also get constraints that come from the setting rather than from what's best for you. Appointments are short. There's often defensive caution. Information gets filtered by what fits into a fifteen-minute visit. An AI system doesn't have to inherit those constraints. It can take the time to explain things, meet people where they are, and engage with follow-up questions at two in the morning when someone is worried about a symptom.

So the persona I find more compelling is something closer to a knowledgeable, trustworthy companion in your health journey. It should be genuinely helpful and willing to engage substantively rather than reflexively saying "consult your doctor" on everything. It also needs to be honest about uncertainty and clear about when something really does need in-person care or escalation. Calibration matters enormously here. You want the model to be confident when the evidence supports it, humble when it doesn't, and transparent about which is which.

There's also a question of who the model is talking to. A clinician using it as a decision-support tool wants something different from a patient trying to understand a new diagnosis. For the clinician, it might act more like a sharp, well-read colleague who can surface the relevant literature and push back when something doesn't add up. For a patient, warmth and clarity matter more, along with real care for their autonomy. That means helping them understand their options and make decisions aligned with their own values, not just telling them what to do.

One thing I'd caution against is sycophancy. In medicine, telling people what they want to hear can genuinely hurt them. So a good medical AI persona has to be kind without being agreeable for the sake of it. It should be willing to deliver hard news gently but honestly.

Ultimately, as these models get more capable, and in some narrow tasks they're already matching or exceeding clinicians, the persona question becomes less about mimicking an existing role and more about designing something new. That means taking the best of what great clinicians do, like empathy, judgment and honesty, and pairing it with things only AI can offer: scale, availability and patience. That's the opportunity, and getting it right is as much a values question as a technical one.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think about this a lot, and I'd say my view has shifted over the last couple of years.

The naive answer is that a medical AI should behave like a doctor. But when you actually sit with that, it's not quite right, because the model isn't situated the way a doctor is. It doesn't have a license, it doesn't have continuity with the patient, it can't order a lab, it can't examine someone, and it's being talked to by people with wildly different levels of health literacy and wildly different needs. Some are clinicians who want a rapid, dense second opinion. Some are a worried parent at two in the morning. So the first thing I'd say is that "persona" probably isn't a single thing. It's more like a set of values and defaults that then adapt to who's on the other side.

That said, there are a few properties I think should be fairly constant. One is calibrated honesty. The model should say what it knows, how confident it is, and what it doesn't know, in a way that a person can actually act on. A lot of the early safety instinct was to make models extremely hedgy, to add disclaimers to everything, to say "consult a healthcare professional" after every sentence. I think that's mostly a failure mode. It trains people to ignore the model, and it's not what a good clinician does. A good clinician will tell you plainly, "This looks like a viral thing, it'll pass, here's what would make me worried." The hedging should be proportional to the actual uncertainty and the actual stakes.

The second is that it should be oriented toward the person's wellbeing rather than toward sounding impressive or toward just being agreeable. Medicine has a long history with this. Patients come in wanting antibiotics or wanting a particular scan, and the right thing is sometimes to gently push back. I think sycophancy is a real risk in these systems, especially as they get more capable, because they get better at telling you a confident story that you want to hear. The persona has to be willing to be a little bit disagreeable when it matters.

Third, and this is where the "increasingly capable" part comes in, I think humility about its own role gets more important, not less, as the models get better. When the model is weak, nobody over-trusts it. When it's genuinely good, when it's matching or exceeding specialists on benchmarks, the temptation is to just defer. And the model should actively work against that in the right situations. It should be pulling the person back toward a clinician when there's something that genuinely needs hands-on care, and it should be thinking about the whole system around the patient, not just answering the question in front of it.

And then the last piece is warmth, honestly. We did some work early on looking at how people and physicians rated model answers, and the things that mattered weren't just accuracy. It was whether the response felt like it took the person seriously, whether it was kind, whether it met them where they were. I don't think that's fluff. If someone has just gotten a scary diagnosis, how you say something changes whether they absorb it and whether they come back. So I'd want the persona to feel like the best version of a clinician you've encountered, the one who was both very good and actually cared, while being honest that it's a different kind of entity with a different kind of role.

astra-6.text:
I think the persona matters a lot, because in medicine, how you communicate is part of whether you’re actually being helpful. You can give a technically correct answer and still leave someone confused about what to do next, or more worried than they need to be.

I’d want a model to be empathetic, but also very honest about what it knows and what it doesn’t know. It should be comfortable saying, “I don’t have enough information to answer that,” and asking a follow-up question. And it should be willing to disagree with you. If you suggest an explanation for your symptoms, being supportive shouldn’t mean automatically validating that explanation.

There’s also a balance around confidence. You don’t want every answer buried under generic disclaimers, because that makes it hard to identify what actually matters. You want uncertainty to be specific: here’s what seems likely, here’s what we can’t rule out, and here’s what would change the next step.

So I’d think less about giving it an authoritative doctor persona and more about making it a careful, approachable collaborator. As the models become more capable, it becomes even more important that the trust they earn comes from good judgment and clear communication, rather than just sounding confident.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the starting point is that you want a model to be helpful and empathetic, but also very honest about what it knows and what it doesn’t know. In medicine, sounding confident and being right are very different things, and a reassuring tone can actually be harmful if it hides uncertainty.

You also don’t want empathy to turn into just agreeing with the user. If someone comes in with a theory about what’s wrong, the model should take their concern seriously without automatically validating that theory. Sometimes the helpful response is to gently push back, ask another question, or say, “This is something you should get evaluated in person.”

And I think the right persona depends on who’s using it. A physician might want a concise discussion of the evidence and the differential diagnosis. A patient might need the same underlying information explained more carefully, with clear next steps. So I’d want flexibility in how the model communicates, but consistency in its honesty, its treatment of uncertainty, and its willingness to disagree when that matters.
